title: Design Patterns
summary: Named, reusable shapes for arranging objects so code stays flexible — and a shared vocabulary that conveys a whole design in one word.

blocks.markdown:
A design pattern is a **named, reusable shape** for arranging objects to solve a recurring problem.

- It's a **template you adapt**, not a library or code you paste.
- Catalogued by the 1994 **Gang of Four**; they named what good designers already did.
- Two ideas run through almost all of them: **program to an interface**, and **favor composition over inheritance**.
- The real payoff is a **shared vocabulary** — "this is a Strategy" conveys the whole layout in one word.

blocks.subTitle: The cheat-sheet
blocks.markdown:
Match the problem to the pattern, not the other way around.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Swap an algorithm at runtime | Strategy |
| Many parts react to one change | Observer |
| Add behavior without subclassing | Decorator |
| Hide a messy subsystem | Facade |
| Many optional construction params | Builder |

Must-knows for interviews: **Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Factory, Builder, Singleton, Adapter, Facade**.

blocks.subTitle: Three families
blocks.markdown:
The 23 GoF patterns split into three buckets by *what problem* they address.

- **Creational** — how objects get made without welding code to a concrete class (Factory, Builder, Singleton).
- **Structural** — how objects compose into bigger structures (Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy).
- **Behavioral** — how objects communicate and divide work (Strategy, Observer, State, Command).

They exist because **change is expensive when everything is glued together** — patterns are what loose coupling looks like.

blocks.subTitle: Strategy
blocks.markdown:
Strategy pulls interchangeable algorithms behind one interface and swaps them at runtime.

- A **Strategy interface** (e.g. `pay(amount)`), several **concrete strategies** (card, PayPal, crypto), and a **context** that holds one and delegates.
- The context **never names a concrete class** — it just calls the interface method.
- Adding an algorithm means **one new class**, touching nothing else.
- Kills sprawling `if/else` chains that get reopened in every feature PR.

blocks.subTitle: Strategy in code
Observer
blocks.markdown:
A subject keeps a list of observers and notifies all of them when something changes.

- The subject exposes `subscribe()` / `unsubscribe()` and loops the list calling `update()`.
- It **doesn't know or care** what observers do — only that they implement the interface.
- Backbone of event systems, UI listeners, and **pub-sub** message queues ([messaging-streaming](messaging-streaming)).
- Add or remove a subscriber without touching the subject.

blocks.subTitle: Decorator
blocks.markdown:
A decorator has the **same interface** as the object it wraps, adds a bit of work, then delegates inward.

- Because it shares the interface, you **stack decorators** to combine features in any order.
- Solves *adding responsibilities dynamically* without a subclass explosion.
- Exactly how `BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(...))` and HTTP middleware stacks work.
- Cost is one extra virtual dispatch — about a **nanosecond**, negligible next to I/O.

blocks.subTitle: Look-alike pairs
blocks.markdown:
Several pairs share a shape but differ in **intent** — interviewers probe exactly this.

| Pair | The difference |
|---|---|
| Strategy vs State | State objects drive transitions; clients pick strategies |
| Decorator vs Proxy | Decorator adds behavior and stacks; proxy controls access |
| Adapter vs Facade | Adapter matches an interface; facade invents a simpler one |

Always answer with "same structure; the *intent* differs".

blocks.subTitle: When to add one
blocks.markdown:
A pattern buys flexibility but costs an interface and an extra hop. Add it only when the problem is present.

- **Growing `if/else` over behaviors** → Strategy. Exactly two fixed cases → a plain `if`.
- **Optional features that combine** → Decorator. One fixed feature → just add a method.
- **Many parts react to one event** → Observer. One consumer → a direct call.
- **Default to the simplest thing**; refactor to a pattern when the *second* variation arrives (YAGNI).

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
These shapes run the frameworks you use daily.

- **Java I/O** — the textbook Decorator: buffering, decoding, file access stacked over one stream interface.
- **Spring** — container-managed Singletons, a giant Factory for beans, dynamic **Proxies** for transactions and security.
- **Kafka** — Observer at network scale: producers are subjects, consumer groups are observers, broker decouples them ([messaging-streaming](messaging-streaming)).
- **UI state libs** — Observer (subscribe and re-render) plus Strategy (pluggable reducers).

blocks.subTitle: Code-health signals
blocks.markdown:
Patterns have no dashboard — the signals live in code review.

- **Adding a variation touches one new file**, not ten → the abstraction is in the right place.
- **You name the pattern and teammates nod** → if a reviewer asks "what's all this indirection for?", it's wrong or premature.
- **Tests construct things in isolation** → if you must spin up the whole world, coupling is too high.
- **Bad signal**: a `XxxFactory` that calls `new` once, or a `XxxStrategy` with one implementation — cargo-cult naming.

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"More patterns = better."** A three-line script wrapped in AbstractFactory + Strategy is worse than the three lines.
- **"Singleton just means one instance."** The danger is the *global access point* — hidden deps, untestable code, thread-safety bugs. Want "one instance, injected".
- **Inheritance to reuse.** It's the rigid, compile-time bond that causes class explosions; composition is the flexible default.
- **Golden Hammer.** Forcing one familiar pattern onto every problem. Match the *problem*, not your habit.
